paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for large instances of the Max-Cut semidefinite program. The optimization variable is a positive semidefinite matrix whose diagonal entries must all equal one. At large sizes, working with this matrix creates a substantial computational and memory challenge, motivating a formulation that supports more economical optimization.

When the cost matrix is positive semidefinite, the authors show an exact reformulation: maximize a smooth concave function over positive semidefinite matrices with unit trace. Exactness means this changes the mathematical form without changing the underlying optimization problem. Applying Frank-Wolfe then produces an algorithm compatible with sampling techniques designed to reduce memory use.

The practical demonstration includes matrices with one million rows and columns and up to five million nonzero cost entries. For diagonally dominant costs, the authors also bound the work needed to reach a specified relative error using randomized approximate eigenvalue computations. Those computations succeed with high probability, giving a qualified computational guarantee alongside the large-scale demonstration.
icml-2023-a-scalable-frank-wolfe-based-a.tldr: An exact reformulation enables a memory-compatible Frank-Wolfe algorithm for very large Max-Cut semidefinite programs.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a single Gaussian distribution can adequately characterize prediction errors for data drawn from a mixture of Gaussian clusters. The setting is generalized linear estimation, with labels produced by a single-index model. The authors derive a sharp expression for training and test errors in a high-dimensional asymptotic regime.

That expression lets them identify both situations where Gaussian universality holds and situations where it fails. Their sufficient conditions depend on how the target weights align with the cluster means and covariances. In plain language, the relationship between the prediction task and the geometry of the data clusters matters for whether a simpler Gaussian description captures the errors.

For least-squares interpolation, the authors establish a strong universality result specifically for training error and give a simple closed-form expression. They also apply their results to real datasets. The contribution is a more precise account of when Gaussian simplification is justified, with distinctions between the general estimation setting and this particular training-error result.
icml-2023-are-gaussian-data-all-you-need.tldr: The paper characterizes when Gaussian mixtures can be replaced by a single Gaussian for error analysis, depending on task–cluster alignment.

paragraphs: Coordinating multiple agents becomes difficult when their observations are incomplete and stochastic. This paper questions the emphasis on training with a centralized true state when agents must ultimately make decentralized decisions. A complete environmental state does not by itself describe the information available to each agent as it decides what to do.

The proposed method, AERIAL, uses attention-based representations of multi-agent recurrence to approximate value functions. It replaces the true state used in state-based centralized training with a learned representation of recurrent agent information. The authors argue that this representation captures information about decentralized decisions more accurately under stochastic partial observability.

The paper also introduces MessySMAC, which modifies SMAC with stochastic observations and greater variation in initial states. This makes the benchmark more configurable for studying the targeted challenge. Evaluations cover Dec-Tiger, SMAC, and MessySMAC, including comparisons with state-based training and robustness checks across stochasticity settings. The stated contribution combines a decision-relevant representation with a benchmark designed to examine it.
icml-2023-attention-based-recurrence-for.tldr: AERIAL uses attention over recurrent agent information to study decentralized coordination under stochastic partial observability.

paragraphs: This paper characterizes neural networks that respect three specified families of symmetry: the orthogonal, special orthogonal, and symplectic groups. Respecting a symmetry means that transforming a layer's input produces the corresponding transformation of its output. The networks considered have layers built from tensor powers of an n-dimensional real vector space, giving the characterization a precise architectural scope.

The central result identifies spanning sets of matrices for the learnable linear maps between these layers. A spanning set provides building blocks whose linear combinations cover every permitted linear equivariant map. This turns an abstract requirement about respecting group transformations into an explicit description of the linear functions a layer can learn.

For the orthogonal and special orthogonal cases, the matrices are expressed in the standard basis; the symplectic case uses a symplectic basis. The contribution is a complete mathematical characterization within the stated layer setting. Its significance lies in describing the full space of allowable linear layers, rather than supplying only selected examples of symmetry-respecting constructions.
icml-2023-brauers-group-equivariant-neur.tldr: The paper characterizes tensor-based equivariant networks for three symmetry groups through explicit spanning sets of linear layer maps.

paragraphs: Program invariants describe properties that hold at relevant points during program execution. Identifying them helps with understanding code, finding bugs, analyzing vulnerabilities, and formal verification. Existing tools discussed in this paper infer invariants from traces collected across multiple executions, so their analysis depends on actually running the program and observing its behavior.

The authors investigate whether large language models can predict invariants directly from source code. They use models trained on code and fine-tuned for invariant generation, allowing the prediction task to be performed statically. Their best-performing approach uses a scratchpad that predicts invariants sequentially through a program, organizing the analysis as a progression through the code.

In the reported study, this static approach produces invariants of quality comparable to a dynamic analysis tool supplied with five program traces. That finding supports code-based invariant prediction as a useful capability of the studied models. The comparison concerns the quality of predicted invariants; it does not turn those predictions into a general guarantee of program correctness.
icml-2023-can-large-language-models-reas.tldr: Code-trained language models can predict program invariants statically, with sequential scratchpads achieving quality comparable to a tool using five execution traces.

paragraphs: Combining several classifiers into an ensemble can benefit generalization, uncertainty estimation, calibration, and adaptation to changing concepts. This paper examines a separate question: what does combining classifiers do to certified robustness? The focus is on mathematical robustness guarantees, so benefits in other aspects of prediction do not automatically settle the question.

The authors introduce S-Lipschitz classifiers as a generalization of Lipschitz continuity. This supplies a framework for analyzing robustness when multiple classifiers are combined. The purpose of the new mathematical description is to identify how ensemble behavior relates to the robustness of the individual classifiers that make it up.

The resulting theory gives precise conditions under which an ensemble of robust classifiers is more robust than every constituent classifier. It also gives conditions under which ensembling reduces robustness. These two directions are central to the contribution: assembling robust components can strengthen a guarantee, but the outcome depends on the conditions governing their combination. The paper makes that dependence explicit through a general certification framework.
icml-2023-certifying-ensembles-a-general.tldr: A generalized Lipschitz framework identifies conditions under which ensembling robust classifiers improves or reduces certified robustness.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model while keeping training data decentralized. This paper addresses how such a system can express uncertainty about its predictions. The authors use conformal prediction, which constructs prediction sets with coverage guarantees under minimal assumptions, and adapt it to a setting with both client differences and privacy constraints.

Their method combines quantile regression with importance weighting. The weighting addresses label shift between agents, meaning that the relative prevalence of labels differs across clients. Accounting for this variation matters because an uncertainty procedure must accommodate the populations represented by the different participants, alongside the requirement to protect their information.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for valid prediction-set coverage and differential privacy within its proposed method. It also reports extensive experiments in which the approach outperforms current competitors. The contribution brings these requirements into one federated uncertainty procedure: handling label imbalance across agents, providing prediction sets with theoretical coverage support, and incorporating a formal privacy guarantee.
icml-2023-conformal-prediction-for-feder.tldr: A federated conformal prediction method uses quantile regression and importance weighting to provide coverage and privacy guarantees under label shift.

paragraphs: A policy can fail after deployment because its environment differs from the one used in training. Some visual differences, such as object color, may be irrelevant to the desired action. Augmenting those features can improve robustness, but a model designer may not know in advance which features an end user's task should ignore.

This paper places the user inside the adaptation process. Its framework generates counterfactual demonstrations that help users isolate changed visual concepts and judge whether those changes should affect the task. When a concept is identified as irrelevant, the system can vary it while retaining existing actions, turning feedback into additional material for fine-tuning.

Experiments with real users cover both discrete and continuous control tasks. The authors report that the full pipeline helps users understand failures, use demonstrations more efficiently during fine-tuning, and adapt the agent to their desired reward. The approach matters because it ties augmentation decisions to the user's understanding of the task, supplying information that may have been unavailable during original training.
icml-2023-diagnosis-feedback-adaptation-.tldr: User feedback on counterfactual demonstrations guides visual augmentation and helps adapt policies to deployment changes.

paragraphs: This paper recasts visual neural networks as dynamical systems following Hamilton's principle. Instead of expressing the network through conventional weights, it uses a finite collection of sub-models with dynamical states. Relations between these states, measured through path integrals, play a role equivalent to ordinary neural weights.

Learning is described through an entropy-reduction process derived from the Euler-Lagrange equations. Feedback acts like stress forces between sub-models, causing their states to move. The authors explore both training a dynamics-based model from scratch and converting pretrained neural structures into this form, then fine-tuning them until their dynamical states stabilize.

The model trained from scratch outperforms traditional neural models on MNIST in the reported experiment. Converted models show consistent improvements over their weight-based counterparts on ImageNet and WebVision in computational complexity, parameter size, test accuracy, and robustness. The authors also report a correlation between structural entropy and model performance. Together, these observations support the proposed dynamical representation as a practical learning approach while connecting its behavior to a structural quantity.
icml-2023-dynamics-inspired-neuromorphic.tldr: A dynamics-based representation replaces conventional neural weights with relations between moving sub-models and shows improvements in visual-learning experiments.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector often assigns each example a numerical score rather than a final normal-or-anomalous decision. Turning those scores into decisions requires a threshold. One way to choose it is to specify the expected fraction of anomalies, called the contamination factor, but that fraction is itself unknown in an unlabeled dataset.

This paper estimates a posterior distribution over the contamination factor using a Bayesian approach. It combines information from several anomaly detectors to capture what appears anomalous, then uses a mixture formulation to infer the contamination level. Producing a distribution makes uncertainty about the fraction of anomalies part of the result, instead of supplying only a single estimate.

Across 22 datasets, the authors find that the estimated distributions are well-calibrated. They also use the posterior mean to set detection thresholds and report better detector performance than several alternative methods. The contribution addresses the decision step between anomaly scores and actionable labels: estimating how many examples to flag, while also representing uncertainty about that quantity.
icml-2023-estimating-the-contamination-f.tldr: A Bayesian method estimates uncertainty in the anomaly fraction and improves detection thresholds in experiments across 22 datasets.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction turns high-dimensional data into a smaller representation that people can visualize and explore. This paper examines how those visualizations can overemphasize relationships between societal phenomena and sensitive attributes or protected groups. Because users explore relationships through the resulting layout, the choice of embedding can shape the associations they see.

The authors introduce the Fair Neighbor Retrieval Visualizer, a framework that treats fair nonlinear dimensionality reduction as an information retrieval task. It evaluates both usefulness and fairness through retrieval criteria. The embedding is optimized to preserve neighborhoods from the original data while avoiding biased associations between those neighborhoods and protected groups.

The reported experiments produce fair visualizations that outperform previous methods. The approach matters because neighborhood preservation and fairness are considered together within the optimization problem. Its target is the representation used for exploration: retaining meaningful local relationships without making protected-group associations disproportionately prominent under the framework's criteria. This gives the fairness objective a direct role in constructing the visual layout.
icml-2023-fair-neighbor-embedding-940181.tldr: Fair Neighbor Embedding optimizes visualizations to preserve data neighborhoods while reducing biased associations with protected groups.

paragraphs: Long-tailed classification involves uneven representation of classes in training data. One proposed response fixes the classifier to an Equiangular Tight Frame, a symmetric geometric arrangement intended to encourage balanced features. This paper argues that symmetry alone does not settle the problem: fixing feature directions may harm generalization even when their arrangement is completely symmetric.

The proposed Representation-Balanced Learning framework introduces orthogonal matrices that let the directions change while preserving the frame's geometry. This separates two design choices that fixed classifiers tie together: the relative structure of the representation and its orientation. The model can therefore learn directions without abandoning the intended balanced arrangement.

The authors theoretically show that RBL's feature learning is insensitive to the training label distribution and learns a balanced representation space. They also analyze generalization through training stability, introducing Two-Parameter Model Stability to handle orthogonally constrained parameters. Experiments report strong performance on several benchmarks with a simple implementation. The central finding is that learning orientation can matter alongside maintaining a balanced geometry.
icml-2023-feature-directions-matter-long.tldr: RBL learns feature directions while preserving symmetric geometry, addressing potential generalization harm from fixed directions in long-tailed classification.

paragraphs: This paper provides a complete characterization of neural networks equivariant to the alternating group, with layers formed from tensor powers of an n-dimensional real vector space. Equivariance requires the network's response to follow the specified symmetry: applying a group transformation to an input must produce the corresponding transformation of the output.

The concrete result is a basis of matrices for learnable linear equivariant maps between those tensor spaces, expressed in the standard basis. A matrix basis identifies independent building blocks that can be combined to express every allowable linear map. This provides an explicit parameterization of the linear layers satisfying the symmetry requirement within the stated architecture family.

The authors also describe how their approach extends to constructing networks with local symmetries. That broadens the construction beyond the initial alternating-group setting. The paper's contribution is structural: it specifies the available symmetry-compatible linear functions completely in its main setting, and explains a route toward applying the same approach when the relevant symmetries are local.
icml-2023-how-jellyfish-characterise-alt.tldr: The paper gives a complete matrix basis for alternating-group-equivariant linear tensor layers and describes an extension to local symmetries.

paragraphs: Attention becomes expensive as sequences grow because its cost scales quadratically with sequence length. This paper introduces Hyena as a subquadratic replacement for attention. Its construction alternates implicitly parameterized long convolutions with data-controlled gates, combining long-range sequence processing with operations whose behavior depends on the input.

The authors evaluate Hyena on reasoning tasks spanning thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens. They report accuracy gains of more than 50 points over the compared state-space, transfer-function, and other implicit and explicit operators, while matching attention-based models. These results address whether lower-cost sequence operators can retain capabilities associated with attention.

On WikiText103 and The Pile, Hyena sets a reported state of the art among architectures without dense attention. It reaches Transformer quality with 20% less training compute at sequence length 2k. Operator measurements show twice the speed of highly optimized attention at 8k and a hundredfold speedup at 64k. These findings distinguish model-quality results from operator-speed measurements while showing advantages at the evaluated sequence lengths.
icml-2023-hyena-hierarchy-towards-larger.tldr: Hyena combines long convolutions and input-dependent gating to match attention-based models in reported evaluations with lower sequence-processing costs.

paragraphs: Adapting a large language model can remain costly even when only a small subset of parameters is tuned, because adaptation still requires gradient-based optimization. HyperTuning instead uses a separate hypermodel to generate task-specific parameters for a fixed downstream model. A few examples provide the task information used to produce those parameters.

The paper implements this idea with HyperT5, a T5-based hypermodel that generates soft prefixes or LoRA parameters for a frozen T5 model. HyperT5 itself undergoes two training stages: an objective that teaches it to generate parameters, followed by multi-task fine-tuning across diverse language tasks. The parameter-generation route therefore relies on a previously trained hypermodel.

Evaluations on P3, MetaICL, and Super-NaturalInstructions show that HyperT5 can generate effective parameters for unseen tasks. The generated parameters also improve performance when used to initialize further parameter-efficient fine-tuning. This gives the approach two demonstrated uses: direct task adaptation through generated parameters, and a starting point for additional optimization when further fine-tuning is desired.
icml-2023-hypertuning-toward-adapting-la.tldr: HyperTuning generates task-specific adaptation parameters from few-shot examples and can also improve initialization for further fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models are widely used to analyze sequences, including sequences with missing data. Standard learning methods, however, rely on knowing where the observations are missing. This paper tackles the harder case in which both the missing values and their positions are unknown, a situation that arises in the natural sciences.

Silent-state HMM methods address related problems but can depend on structural restrictions such as an acyclic underlying chain. The authors develop reconstruction algorithms that require no assumptions about the chain's structure and can operate with limited prior knowledge. Removing that structural requirement expands the kinds of sequential processes the algorithms can address.

The evaluation examines reconstruction precision across multiple scenarios and robustness when the model is misspecified. Under proper specifications, the authors show that process dynamics can be reconstructed as well as when the missing positions are known. The qualification matters: the finding identifies circumstances where unknown deletion locations need not degrade reconstruction, alongside an investigation of behavior when the model specification is imperfect.
icml-2023-learning-hidden-markov-models-.tldr: New HMM reconstruction algorithms handle unknown missing-observation locations without structural assumptions on the underlying chain.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear convolutional neural networks as a tractable step toward understanding CNN learning. By analyzing gradient descent, the authors connect training behavior to the interaction between the dataset's statistical structure and the network's convolutional structure. The resulting account makes both the data and the architecture central to explaining what is learned.

They show that discoveries of statistical structure occur through ordered, stage-like transitions, even though the network itself is linear. The speed of those discoveries depends on the relationship between dataset and network structure. They also identify a dominant frequency bias: the network makes these discoveries using only the dominant frequencies associated with different structural parts of the data.

Experiments examine how the theory relates to deep nonlinear CNNs used in practice. The authors suggest that the findings can help explain shortcut learning and a preference for texture over shape. The theoretical result concerns linear CNNs, while the experiments provide a connection to more complex networks and the interpretation offers a possible explanation of their behavior.
icml-2023-linear-cnns-discover-the-stati.tldr: A theory of linear CNNs links staged learning and dominant-frequency bias to interactions between dataset structure and convolutional architecture.

paragraphs: Many 3D molecule generators first place atoms and then assign chemical bonds afterward. The difficulty is that atom positions generated without considering bonds may admit no compatible bond assignment. This paper calls that failure atom-bond inconsistency and argues that it is a main cause of unrealistic molecules produced by existing approaches.

MolDiff addresses the issue by generating atoms and bonds simultaneously with a diffusion model. It explicitly models their dependence so that the two parts of the molecular representation remain consistent during generation. This brings chemical connectivity into the generative process instead of leaving it entirely to a post-processing stage after atom placement.

The authors evaluate both generation ability and molecular quality using criteria covering geometry and chemical properties. Their empirical study reports a threefold improvement in success rate over previous approaches, together with significantly better molecule quality. The findings support joint atom-and-bond modeling as a way to improve the consistency of generated structures. The claim that inconsistency is the main underlying cause remains the authors' stated explanation.
icml-2023-moldiff-addressing-the-atom-bo.tldr: MolDiff jointly generates atoms and bonds to address inconsistent 3D molecules, reporting a threefold improvement in generation success rate.

paragraphs: Flow-matching methods train continuous-time generative models using probability paths connecting noise to data. Existing approaches can construct paths that are optimal for individual samples, but independently pairing noise and data leaves structure across the data distribution unused. This paper studies how more deliberate relationships between samples can improve the resulting flow.

Multisample Flow Matching introduces couplings between noise and data samples while preserving the required marginal distributions. In other words, the pairing changes while the individual noise and data distributions remain correct. The framework retains simulation-free training and a simple minimization objective, with a small additional computational overhead.

The authors report reduced gradient variance, straighter learned flows, and low-cost transport maps in high dimensions. Straighter flows allow high-quality generation with fewer function evaluations, linking the training construction to sampling efficiency. Experiments on downsampled ImageNet show improved sample consistency and better low-cost generation. The transport-map result also gives the framework potential uses beyond generation, while the empirical findings support the benefits of coordinating sample pairings.
icml-2023-multisample-flow-matching-stra.tldr: Multisample Flow Matching couples noise and data samples to reduce training variance and learn straighter, cheaper-to-sample generative flows.

paragraphs: Independence testing asks whether two quantities are statistically related. Traditional batch tests fix the sample size before data collection, while practitioners may want to keep collecting evidence until the problem is resolved. Repeatedly checking a batch test requires multiple-testing corrections to preserve validity, which can reduce its ability to detect dependence.

This paper develops sequential kernelized independence tests using the principle of testing by betting. Evidence can be incorporated as observations arrive, supporting continuous monitoring while controlling false alarms. The framework includes betting strategies inspired by kernel-based dependence measures, including the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion.

The aim is to adapt data collection to difficulty: easy cases can stop earlier, while harder ones can accumulate more evidence. The authors also establish validity in non-independent, non-identically distributed time-varying settings and demonstrate statistical power on simulated and real data. The contribution joins flexible stopping with a framework for measuring dependence, addressing the mismatch between fixed-sample procedures and the way evidence is often gathered in practice.
icml-2023-sequential-kernelized-independ.tldr: Betting-based kernel tests support sequential independence testing with continuous evidence updates and false-alarm control.

paragraphs: This paper examines the geometry behind neural-network optimization and representation. Neural networks can have many parameter settings corresponding to the same output, while the collection of outputs they can produce has a complicated shape. These properties motivate studying the loss landscape and the functions an architecture can represent as related mathematical questions.

The first result gives an explicit bound on hidden-layer sizes sufficient to rule out spurious valleys in the loss landscape. The authors connect this condition to the success of gradient descent methods. The result supplies a concrete architectural condition for favorable optimization geometry; it is a sufficient width bound rather than a claim that every smaller architecture must fail.

The second result introduces a method for determining whether an architecture with monomial activations can represent a target function. It studies a particular set of error values and how that set changes with training datasets. Together, the results address both reaching good solutions through optimization and determining whether the desired function lies within an architecture's representational possibilities.
icml-2023-spurious-valleys-and-clusterin.tldr: The paper gives sufficient layer-width bounds for eliminating spurious valleys and a representability analysis for networks with monomial activations.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to solve tasks introduced one after another. Learning a new task can damage performance on earlier ones, producing catastrophic forgetting. Practical approaches address this through memory, regularization, or model expansion, but this paper argues that their theoretical relationships and behavior need a clearer common foundation.

The proposed Ideal Continual Learner framework avoids catastrophic forgetting by construction. The authors show that it unifies several established continual-learning methods, allowing their strengths and weaknesses to be examined through a shared theoretical lens. The guarantee belongs to the constructed framework, while the unification provides a way to understand existing approaches.

The paper also derives generalization bounds that quantify how rehearsal affects generalization. This moves the analysis beyond whether earlier tasks are retained to how revisiting prior material relates to performance beyond the observed examples. Connections to classic and modern research topics provide additional context and possible future directions. The main contribution is a theoretical organizing framework with explicit forgetting and generalization results.
icml-2023-the-ideal-continual-learner-an.tldr: The Ideal Continual Learner unifies established methods in a framework that avoids catastrophic forgetting and quantifies rehearsal's effect on generalization.

paragraphs: A common approach to learning control alternates between estimating system dynamics and optimizing a policy using the estimated model. This paper rigorously studies a simplified version of that approach for nonlinear systems. Its question is whether repeatedly learning manageable local models can support policy improvement with a controlled amount of data.

The algorithm estimates local linear approximations to nonlinear dynamics and then performs policy updates resembling iterative linear quadratic regulation. These approximations describe the dynamics locally, allowing the procedure to combine model learning with trajectory-oriented optimization. A key part of the analysis is the construction of locally stabilizing gains.

The authors show polynomial sample complexity in the relevant problem parameters. By incorporating local stabilization, the method overcomes exponential dependence on the planning horizon, addressing a major source of difficulty in longer control problems. Experiments validate the algorithm's performance and compare it with deep-learning baselines. The contribution provides theoretical support for the analyzed local-model strategy, alongside empirical evidence for its use in nonlinear policy optimization.
icml-2023-the-power-of-learned-locally-l.tldr: An analyzed policy-optimization algorithm learns local linear dynamics and uses stabilization to avoid exponential horizon dependence in sample complexity.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo reinforcement learning often spends a fixed interaction budget on simulated episodes of equal length. This paper questions that allocation when the objective discounts future rewards. Earlier rewards contribute more heavily to discounted return, so collecting the same number of observations at every trajectory depth may use the budget inefficiently.

The authors design a budget-allocation strategy chosen in advance that collects trajectories of different lengths. Some simulations are truncated, changing how interaction effort is distributed across early and late steps. They prove that the proposed allocation minimizes the width of confidence intervals around empirical estimates of a policy's expected return.

The truncation mechanism is then incorporated into Policy Optimization via Importance Sampling, and the resulting algorithm is compared numerically with the original POIS method. The results agree with the theory and show that appropriate truncation can improve performance. The practical message is that trajectory length is a meaningful part of experimental design: allocating the same budget differently can improve return estimation and, in the reported comparisons, policy optimization.
icml-2023-truncating-trajectories-in-mon.tldr: Allocating simulation budgets across unequal trajectory lengths tightens return-estimation confidence intervals and can improve policy optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover unknown terms in differential equations from sparse measurements. Prior knowledge of the dynamics helps make the small-data problem tractable. The Universal Physics-Informed Neural Network approach extends physics-informed learning by adding a neural network specifically tasked with representing hidden terms in the equation.

The method produces two outputs: a surrogate solution to the differential equation and a learned, initially black-box description of its unknown terms. Symbolic regression tools such as AI Feynman can then convert the hidden-term representation into symbolic equations. This separates fitting the missing dynamics from expressing them in an interpretable mathematical form.

To obtain convergence, the authors provide noisy measurements of initial conditions together with synthetic experimental observations at later times. Their demonstrations show strong performance with very few noisy measurements in both ordinary and partial differential equation settings. The stated data setup is important: the approach combines prior dynamical information with observations over time, using that combination to reconstruct solutions and support symbolic discovery of unknown operators.
icml-2023-universal-physics-informed-neu.tldr: Universal PINNs learn unknown differential-equation terms from sparse noisy observations and enable their conversion into symbolic equations.
